老熊隨筆 case study, September 2026

Find me on my own timeline

Meta’s brand-new Muse agent crawled twelve years of my Facebook looking for solo pictures of me. What came back is a small classification experiment: four clean hits, one honest “maybe,” and one lesson about trusting captions.

By 老熊 (Chang-Meng Hsiung)

The whole haul, marked up the way we used to mark proof sheets.

Contents

  1. The ask
  2. The crawl
  3. The caption trap
  4. “Just the most likely ones”
  5. The honest maybe
  6. The scorecard
  7. 復盤: what I’d tell a friend

1The ask

Earlier this month Meta launched Muse, its personal agent built on the Muse Spark models and wired straight into your Facebook and Instagram. A new tool deserves a real test, and for a retired chemometrician the obvious test is a classification problem where I already hold the ground truth.

So I gave it one job.

Find the solo pictures of me in my Facebook.

For a person, that is trivial. I know which ones they are. For an agent, it is three problems stacked on top of each other: read a long timeline, separate real photographs from everything else, and then tell one man standing alone from a crowd, a meme, a plate of food, or somebody else entirely.

↑ 回目錄

2The crawl

Muse’s first report was brisk and, I have to admit, a little too well informed.

Muse

I crawled your entire timeline — 2,439 posts going back to 2014, with 991 photo posts. After filtering out link previews and text-heavy screenshots (most of your recent posts are screenshots of AI chats), there are about 864 real photos to look through.

Guilty on the AI chats. Then came the line that mattered more than all the numbers before it.

Muse

One snag: my photo viewer hit a failure partway through, so I couldn’t actually look at the photos themselves yet — which is the whole point, since only looking can tell a solo shot of you from a group photo or a meme.

Posts on the timeline, back to 20142,439
Photo posts991
Real photos after filtering~864
Photos actually looked at, first pass0

Credit where it is due: Muse reported its own failure instead of papering over it, and it named exactly why the failure mattered. A lot of software, and a fair number of people, would have skipped that sentence.

3The caption trap

Even blind, Muse offered one “confirmed” find.

Muse

One confirmed find from your own caption, though: your June 8 post about the KMT event photos says you attached one of your solo photos （獨照）.

Read that again: from your own caption. The confirmation came from my words, not from any picture. And the picture that came back from that post looks like this.

Thirty-odd people behind a red 北加州中華耆英聯合會 banner, flags in hand. Whatever the caption promised was somewhere in that post, this frame is about as far from a solo as a photograph gets.

In spectroscopy we have a name for this mistake: trusting the label on the bottle instead of the spectrum. The label is metadata. It tells you what somebody believed when they wrote it. Only the measurement tells you what is actually in the bottle.

↑ 回目錄

4“Just the most likely ones”

Muse then offered to go through all 864 candidates visually, in the background. It gave me two buttons. I took the lazy one.

Just the most likely ones

Muse

Went through all 36 photos — here are the solo ones of you, confirmed by sight.

Thirty-six of roughly 864, about four percent of the pile, and four solos out of the thirty-six. This time the claim was “confirmed by sight,” so I audited each one against the pixels. Here they are in the order they were taken, not the order they were posted.

Taken November 23, 2012; posted November 26, 2022

Muse said

Nov 26, 2022 (photo from ~2012) — standing solo in the Santa Clara University chapel.

Audit

Correct, and the nicest catch of the day. The post is from 2022, but Muse read the camera’s burned-in stamp, 11/23/2012 15:12, and dated the photo rather than the post. That is the difference between when a sample was logged and when it was measured.

August 17, 2015

Muse said

Full-body hotel-room selfie, wave t-shirt and red shorts.

Audit

Correct on everything that matters. One pedantic note: it is not a selfie. One hand is on the wall and the other is on my hip, so somebody else was holding the camera. Solo, yes. Selfie, no.

August 23, 2020

Muse said

Mirror selfie after your wife’s third pandemic haircut.

Audit

Correct. No model reads a haircut count off a scalp, so “third” came from my caption. The difference from the June 8 post is that here the caption and the pixels agree. That is how metadata should be used: as a second witness, never the only one. 田總’s handiwork, for the record, holds up.

January 28, 2023

Muse said

Mirror selfie in a blue/pink button-up, around your company new-year gathering.

Audit

Correct. Patchwork shirt, plaid pocket, gold phone, the classic two-handed mirror grip. The occasion is Muse reading my post; the solo call is Muse reading the picture, and the picture is unambiguous.

5The honest maybe

Then Muse added a line I did not expect.

Muse

One honest maybe: the Dec 23, 2024 cap selfie in front of the Sphere — no glasses, looks younger, so I’d guess family rather than you, but worth a glance if you want. Everything else was groups, food, scenery, or animals.

find this: the Dec 23, 2024 cap selfie in front of the Sphere

Muse

Here it is — Dec 23, 2024, caption 就住大球隔壁 哈哈 (“living right next to the big ball”).

Muse

Looking again — no glasses, much younger than your other selfies, so I’m fairly confident it’s a family member rather than you.

This was the best moment of the session. The photo sits on my timeline, under my account, with a jokey first-person caption. A system that trusted metadata the way it did on June 8 would have filed it straight into the solo pile. Instead Muse looked at the pixels, noticed two features that did not fit the other four frames (no glasses, and an age gap measured in decades), and declined to make the call. It did not silently drop the frame and it did not silently include it. It put the case in front of me and said how sure it was.

I have spent a good part of my career, three issued patents’ worth, on classifiers that know when to say “I’m not sure.” In chemometrics we call it abstention, and a model that can abstain is worth more than one that is always confident. It was a pleasure to watch a consumer agent do it unprompted. The verdict stands: the young man under the cap is not in my solo collection.

7復盤: what I’d tell a friend

Ask what “confirmed” means. When an agent says it found something, ask whether it confirmed the thing itself or somebody’s description of it. Muse was perfect when it looked and wrong the one time it only read. It even told me which was which; I just had to notice the words “from your own caption.”

“Most likely” is a sample, not a census. Four percent of the pile produced four good solos. The other ninety-six percent may hold more, and the only way to know is to say yes to the long pass.

The honest behaviors are the valuable ones. Reporting a broken photo viewer, offering the long pass instead of pretending to have done it, and flagging the Sphere as a maybe: none of those is flashy, and all of them are what make the four hits believable.

Know what you paid. To do a job I could have done myself in an afternoon, Muse read twelve years of my posts, captions, and photos, and teased me about my AI-chat screenshots along the way. That access is the whole feature. It is worth deciding, before you ask, that you are comfortable with it.

For a tool a few weeks old, this is a respectable first run. I would trust its eyes. I would double-check its reading.
